catalog_quote: Sri Lanka Malay words do not show different levels of prominence in their syllables, neither phonologically nor phonetically. In other words, there is no word accent or stress. Smith et al. (2004) claim that “stress falls on the long vowel of a word, or on the initial syllable if the word only contains only short vowels.” They do not state by which acoustic cue they established the location of stress, so that we are probably dealing with an impressionistic statement here. Bakker (2006) reports accent on the first syllable, drawing on Robuchon (2003). These statements again seem to be impressionistic. Some instrumental analyses were undertaken to check these claims, but no cues for a saliently prominent (stressed) syllable could be found. 49 words with different syllable structures were checked in 6 different controlled environments with two male native speakers of SLM for pitch contour …
sweep_summary: One sweep item (Apoussidou & Nordhoff 2008, OCP5 Toulouse talk): existence verified on the archived OCP5 programme (Fri 25 Jan 2008, 15h00), but no abstract, handout or slides exist anywhere open (booklet never posted; author pages, Crossref, LingBuzz, OpenAlex/S2, Scholar, Bing all empty or blocked; Its findings are reported first-hand by the same authors in the catalog's deciding source, Nordhoff 2009 (LOT 226), which was fetched sources from LOT and read: catalog quote verified verbatim at sec. 4.4.5 p. 117; instrumental study finds no pitch/intensity prominence cue, duration and vowel quality rejected as stress cues, vowel length analysed by extrametricality + bimoraic foot (sec. 4.5), SLM framed as stressless like its Malayic/Javanese input languages (sec. 4.5.4). Catalog coding NO-WORD-STRESS confirmed; nothing supersedes Nordhoff 2009. Files and / under

new_statements.quote: Sri Lanka Malay words do not show different levels of prominence in their syllables, neither phonologically nor phonetically. In other words, there is no word accent or stress. [...] Some instrumental analyses were undertaken to check these claims, but no cues for a saliently prominent (stressed) syllable could be found. 49 words with different syllable structures were checked in 6 different controlled environments with two male native speakers of SLM for pitch contour and intensity. The compiled measurements taken together do not suggest that a meaningful generalization about the correlation between word structure and pitch or intensity can be made (Apoussidou & Nordhoff 2008).

new_statements.reading: Sri Lanka Malay has no word stress or accent: the author's own instrumental study (with Apoussidou; 49 words, 6 environments, 2 male speakers) finds no pitch or intensity cue of prominence; duration is rejected as a cue (long vowels are explained instead by final-syllable extrametricality plus a bimoraic-foot requirement, sec. 4.5), and vowel quality only marks the root antepenult as non-prominent without picking out a prominent syllable (p. 120). Earlier impressionistic claims (Smith et al. 2004: stress on the long vowel, else initial; Bakker 2006 / Robuchon 2003: initial accent) are explicitly rejected. This is the catalog's existing deciding source; the quote is verified verbatim at p. 117.
